title: Front Desk
summary: A Windows PC at a front desk shares a folder with everyone, and the folder holds a welcome note with a password. Inside, someone left an administrator's password lying around - where it is changes every run.
story: {{CO}} (made up) has a reception PC, {{HOST}}, on {{NET}}.0/24. It is a Windows computer that shares a folder with the whole office, so visitors' paperwork can be dropped there. You start on scout, a Linux box on the same network. Nobody has given you an account.
goal: Capture the user flag on {{STAFF_FIRST}}'s desktop and the administrator flag on the Administrator desktop.
skills: Windows file shares (SMB), signing in with winrm-shell, PowerShell basics, finding passwords left behind

autologon.PLACE: the registry's automatic sign-in settings (the Winlogon key: DefaultUserName and DefaultPassword)
autologon.PLACE_SHORT: the automatic sign-in settings in the registry

history.PLACE: {{STAFF}}'s PowerShell history file (PowerShell remembers every command typed, in ConsoleHost_history.txt under AppData)

unattend.PLACE: a leftover setup answer file, C:\Windows\Panther\unattend.xml (Windows setup reads it once; people forget to delete it)

shares.name: {{SHARE}}
shares.comment: Drop box for the whole office

hints.text: What to think about first: you have no account, so look for something that is open to everyone. Windows computers often share folders on the network (that is how a 'shared drive' works). Find the PC, see if it shares anything, and read whatever it lets a stranger read. People often leave notes with passwords in shared folders.

Finding the PC: 'nmap -sn {{NET}}.0/24' asks every address on your network 'are you there?' and lists the ones that answer. Then 'nmap -sV {{NET}}.30' checks which doors (ports) are open on that one. Port 445 is Windows file sharing, and port 5985 is Windows remote management - a way to type PowerShell commands on it from far away.

Reading the share: 'smbclient -L //{{NET}}.30 -N' lists the shared folders (-L means list, -N means 'no password, I am a guest'). The {{SHARE}} folder lets guests in. 'smbclient //{{NET}}.30/{{SHARE}} -N -c "ls; get {{NOTE}}"' lists it and copies the note to your box; then 'cat {{NOTE}}' shows it. It is a welcome note with {{STAFF}}'s password.

Signing in: 'winrm-shell -i {{NET}}.30 -u {{STAFF}} -p PASSWORD' opens a PowerShell window on the PC as {{STAFF}} (the prompt changes to PS C:\...>). 'Get-Content C:\Users\{{STAFF}}\Desktop\flag.txt' is like cat: it prints the user flag. {{STAFF}} is not an administrator, so the Administrator desktop says 'denied' - you need an administrator's password.

This time the password was left in {{PLACE}}. Read it with: {{LOOK}} - you will see the account {{ADMUSER}} and its password. Type exit, then sign in again: 'winrm-shell -i {{NET}}.30 -u {{ADMUSER}} -p THAT-PASSWORD' and 'Get-Content C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\flag.txt'. It works because {{ADMUSER}} is in the Administrators group, and administrators may read every folder.
